**Session or topic covered: Introduction to Time Series**

Coming into the first lesson of the semester, I had a very basic understanding of what time series was. In the first lecture we covered the foundational definitions, such as the ordering of observations, the types of time series we can get, the spacing between observations, and how dependence can be made visible. The most challenging concept for me this week was definitely temporal regularity and the aggregation effect. At first I didn't understand the idea of aggregation smoothing out high-frequency structure, or how changing the level of aggregation reveals different structure in the series. The wording was quite complicated and confusing, so I did some research until I understood exactly what it meant. When I feel confused about a topic, I usually ask AI to explain the concept not just mathematically or statistically but intuitively, so that I can understand the idea in a simple way and then build it up into a deeper understanding.

I now understand that granularity is about the resolution we look at the data in. As the granularity changes, different patterns become visible, and focusing on a finer level of detail lets us see patterns that are hidden at a coarser level. For example, hourly temperature data shows the fluctuations throughout the day, while daily data only shows the average temperature for each day. The temperature itself doesn't behave any differently; we are just seeing a different level of detail. That is what the idea that nothing changes about the underlying process, only what we see changes, means to me now.

During class we discussed the difference between prediction and forecasting, which I initially found confusing. After doing some research, I now understand forecasting as a specific type of prediction. Both involve using available information to estimate an unknown quantity, but forecasting specifically focuses on estimating a future value, often by using historical time series data and assuming that patterns observed in the past may continue into the future. Prediction is a broader concept and does not necessarily involve time or historical data.

From the introduction to time series, I think one of the most important conversations we had in class was around goals and planning. The loop from forecasting to goal, to plan, to implementation, to outcome is important for understanding the life cycle of a forecast. It helped me understand how to go about setting a goal and planning how to organise and manage the data, which I think will be very helpful when dealing with major projects.
